title: Question 13
stem: Outline the principles of computed tomography (CT scanning).

parts.text: Outline the principles of computed tomography (CT scanning).

markscheme_points.text: X-ray image of a (single) slice/cross-section (through the patient)
computer is used to form/process/build up/store image

hints: Hint 1: Start by remembering what an ordinary X-ray shows and what its big limitation is when all the organs overlap on one flat film.
Hint 2: Think how you could look at just one thin slice through the body instead of the whole thickness at once.
Hint 3: Consider why taking just one view of that slice is not enough, and what moving the X-ray tube around the patient would give you.
Hint 4: Recall what happens to X-ray intensity as it passes through bone, muscle and air, and what the detectors on the opposite side must record.
Hint 5: Think about what is needed to combine hundreds of different attenuation readings from different angles into a clear picture.
Hint 6: Imagine you have clear 2D pictures of many thin slices side by side, and think how you could use them to see the whole volume.
parts.proper_answer: CT scanning produces an X-ray image of a single thin slice / cross-section through the patient. A collimated X-ray beam and detectors rotate around the patient so the slice is viewed from many different angles. Transmitted intensities are recorded, giving attenuation data for each direction. A computer processes all the data to build up a 2D image of the slice. The procedure is repeated for many neighbouring slices and the slices are combined to form a 3D image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why a Slice, Not a Shadow**
Think with me about a normal X-ray. The beam goes right through your whole chest and everything - ribs, heart, lungs - overlaps on one film. It is hard to see detail. In CT we do something cleverer. We collimate the beam into a thin fan so it only illuminates one thin slice or cross-section through you at a time.

Step 2: **Looking From All Around**
One view of that slice still is not enough. So the X-ray tube and an array of detectors rotate together around the patient in the plane of the slice. At each angle a short pulse of X-rays is sent through the slice and the transmitted intensity is measured.

Step 3: **What the Detectors Are Really Measuring**
Remember, different tissues attenuate X-rays differently: $$I = I_{0}e^{-\mu x}$$ where $\mu$ is the attenuation coefficient. Bone has large $\mu$ and absorbs a lot, soft tissue has medium $\mu$, air spaces have very small $\mu$. So for every beam direction the detector records how much was absorbed along that path.

Step 4: **Let the Computer Build the 2D Picture**
You now have hundreds of attenuation readings from all angles around the same slice. No person could combine these by hand. A computer stores and processes all this data and works out the value of $\mu$ at each small point in the slice. It then displays this as a detailed 2D image of that slice, with contrast between bone, soft tissue and air.

Step 5: **From Many Slices to a 3D Volume**
That gives you just one slice. The patient is then moved a small step along, and the whole rotating scan is repeated for the next neighbouring slice. Do this many times and the computer stacks all the 2D slice images together to build up a complete 3D image of the organ or region, which can be rotated and viewed from any direction.
